title: Italian Game · A practical Black repertoire
description: Develop with Bc5 and meet White's common fourth moves, choose a plan after castling, meet the early d4 break and the Nc3 gambit, and decline the Evans Gambit. Guided decisions connect the moves to their resulting positions.

credits.text: Original Fieldwork instruction and annotations. Historical game scores are credited separately.

notes.text: White pushes d4 before castling. Black must account for the attack on e5 and c5.
Bb4+ saves the attacked bishop with check; White must answer before carrying on with the center.
With White's knight on c3, d5 attacks both the e4-pawn and c4-bishop.
This game used Nc3 rather than our Bd2 reply and bishop exchange. Black developed Be6 here; treat the later play as an example to inspect, not a continuation of your recall line.
The recorded game ends at Rxh7+. Von Bardeleben left the room instead of resigning and lost on time. This is check, not the final position of a played checkmate.

steps.title: The Italian, with Black
steps.text: Meet e4 with a share of the center, develop your pieces and make your king safe. We use Bc5 against the Italian, then adjust to White's plan. These are selected study moves, not the only good replies.

steps.title: White opens the center
steps.text: White begins with e4. You play Black throughout this course.

steps.title: Claim your share
steps.text: Put your e-pawn in the center and open the f8-bishop's diagonal.
steps.feedback: e5 contests d4 and f4. White develops Nf3 and attacks your pawn.

steps.title: Defend while developing
steps.text: Develop your queenside knight to defend e5.
steps.feedback: Nc6 protects e5. White's Bc4 now points toward f7: this is the Italian.

steps.title: Choose the bishop-first setup
steps.text: Place your kingside bishop on the diagonal toward f2 and clear part of the castling route.
steps.feedback: Bc5 clears f8 for castling. Now White chooses a plan.

steps.title: If White castles
steps.text: White has several common fourth moves. This chapter's main line is d3; side trips show castling, Nc3, Ng5 and d4 first, and later chapters cover c3 and the Evans Gambit, b4. Explore castling, or continue to the next reply.

steps.title: White castles first
steps.text: White puts the king away before choosing a pawn setup. Carry on developing.

steps.title: Develop with an attack
steps.text: Develop your kingside knight toward the center, where it attacks e4.
steps.feedback: Nf6 attacks e4, and White defends it with d3. This is the main line's position, reached in a different order.

steps.title: Keep e5 supported
steps.text: Support your e-pawn and free the c8-bishop's diagonal, as in the main line.
steps.feedback: d6 supports e5, exactly as in the main line.

steps.title: Back on familiar ground
steps.text: If White plays c3 next, castle: you are back in the main line. Against Bg5, h3 or Nc3, play h6 first; against Ng5, castle. Earlier, against Ng5 instead of d3, castle too, and against Nc3 or Re1, d6 was still the move. If White had played c3 instead of d3, nothing defended e4: take it with Nxe4, and answer d4 with d5. Against d4 instead of d3, take with the bishop: after Bxd4 Nxd4 Nxd4 you are a pawn ahead.

steps.title: If White plays Nc3
steps.text: Explore Nc3, or continue to the next reply.

steps.title: White develops the queenside knight
steps.text: Nc3 develops and defends e4. It also blocks White's c-pawn, so White cannot build a c3 and d4 center.

steps.title: Develop the other knight
steps.text: Develop your kingside knight toward the center.
steps.feedback: Nf6 develops and attacks e4. White adds a second defender with d3.

steps.title: Keep e5 supported
steps.text: Support your e-pawn and free the c8-bishop's diagonal.
steps.feedback: d6 supports e5. Castling comes next, as in the main line.

steps.title: Watch for a fork trick
steps.text: Castle next. If White pins your f6-knight with Bg5, attack the bishop with h6; against Be3, trade bishops with Bxe3. Earlier, if White had castled instead of playing d3, d6 was still the move; against Ng5, castle. If White had grabbed e5 with Nxe5, take the knight: Nxe5. Then d4 forks your bishop and knight, but Nxc4 takes White's bishop first, and after dxc5 you are a piece for a pawn ahead.

steps.title: If White plays Ng5
steps.text: Explore Ng5, an early attack on f7, or continue to the next reply.

steps.title: White attacks f7 at once
steps.text: Ng5 joins the c4-bishop against f7 and threatens Nxf7, forking your queen and h8-rook. Before you defend, check what protects the knight.

steps.title: Take the undefended knight
steps.text: Nothing defends the g5-knight. Capture it.
steps.feedback: Your queen wins a whole knight. White's d4 attacks your c5-bishop and opens the c1-bishop's path to your queen.
steps.hint: Move the queen from d8 to g5.

steps.title: Move the queen with a gain
steps.text: Your queen is attacked. Move it to a square where it takes a pawn and attacks a rook.
steps.feedback: Qxg2 wins a pawn and attacks the h1-rook.
steps.hint: Capture on g2 with the queen.

steps.title: A piece ahead
steps.text: If White takes your bishop with dxc5, take the rook with check: Qxh1+. If the rook steps to f1 instead, Qxe4+ takes another pawn with check. Earlier, if White had played d3 instead of d4, take on g2 just the same. If White had castled, simply keep your queen safe: you are a knight ahead.

steps.title: If White plays d4
steps.text: Explore d4, which strikes at the center at once, or continue to the main line.

steps.title: White strikes in the center
steps.text: d4 attacks your c5-bishop. Count the d4-pawn's attackers and defenders: your e5-pawn, bishop and knight against White's knight and queen.

steps.title: Take with the bishop
steps.text: Capture the d4-pawn with the attacked bishop.
steps.feedback: Bxd4 takes the pawn. White trades knight for bishop with Nxd4.
steps.hint: Capture on d4 with the bishop from c5.

steps.title: Take back
steps.text: Recapture the knight on d4.
steps.feedback: You are a pawn ahead: the minor pieces are even, and White's d-pawn is gone. White's c3 attacks your knight.
steps.hint: Capture on d4 with the knight from c6.

steps.title: Bring the knight back
steps.text: Retreat the attacked knight to c6, where it guards e5 again.
steps.feedback: Nc6 is safe and defends e5. But White's Qf3 lines up with the c4-bishop against f7 and threatens Qxf7, checkmate.
steps.hint: Move the knight from d4 to c6.

steps.title: Stop the mate
steps.text: Defend f7 with your queen. A queen trade would suit you, since you are a pawn ahead.
steps.feedback: Qf6 defends f7. If White trades queens, recapture with the g8-knight, which develops it.
steps.hint: Move the queen from d8 to f6.

steps.title: A pawn ahead
steps.text: Next, develop your g8-knight and castle. If White's queen had gone to d5 instead of f3, it threatens the same mate, and Qf6 defends again. Earlier, if White had attacked f7 with Ng5 instead of taking your bishop, defend with Nh6; if White had attacked the bishop with c3, retreat it to b6. If White had brought the queen to h5 instead of playing c3, Qe7 guards both f7 and e5; if White had attacked your knight with Be3, bring it back to c6.

steps.title: White supports the center
steps.text: White supports e4 with d3; no central pawns have been exchanged yet.

steps.title: Bring out the other knight
steps.text: Develop your kingside knight toward the center.
steps.feedback: Nf6 attacks e4, but d3 protects it. This is development, not a free pawn. Your bishop and knight have now cleared the route for castling.

steps.title: What if White attacks f7?
steps.text: White need not castle next. You can inspect Ng5 and a useful defensive purpose of castling, or continue with White's quiet plan.

steps.title: White attacks f7
steps.text: Ng5 joins the c4-bishop in attacking f7 and threatens Nxf7, forking your queen and h8-rook.

steps.title: Castle to reinforce f7
steps.text: Castle: the rook comes from h8 to f8, adding a defender while making the king safer.
steps.feedback: Your king and the f8-rook now both defend f7.
steps.hint: Castle kingside by moving e8 to g8.

steps.title: Check the defenders, not just the threat
steps.text: The rook on f8 and king on g8 now defend f7. If White captures there with the knight, Rxf7 is available. This is why the bishop-first move order matters: you can castle after developing Nf6. Return to the quiet line when ready.

steps.title: White chooses the quiet plan
steps.text: White castles instead of attacking f7. Now support your center and complete your own king safety.

steps.title: Keep e5 supported
steps.text: Support your e-pawn and free the c8-bishop's diagonal.
steps.feedback: d6 supports e5. White's c3 prepares d4, so watch for the center opening next.

steps.title: Make the king safe
steps.text: Your kingside pieces are out of the way. Castle before choosing a longer plan.
steps.feedback: The king reaches g8 and the rook f8. Castling is a checkpoint, not the end of your opening plan: the c8-bishop still needs a job.

steps.title: Lasker develops against a quiet Italian
steps.text: Mason–Lasker, Hastings 1895. White chooses Nc3 and Be3 instead of our quick castle. Follow Black's development and notice what exchanging on e3 changes. This example is not extra recall material.

steps.title: Build your Black setup
steps.text: Play the line you just learned.

steps.title: Castling is the starting point for a plan
steps.text: Begin from the quiet setup you learned earlier. Both kings are safe, but your c8-bishop is undeveloped. This chapter connects three choices: restrain White's queenside expansion, challenge the active bishop, and understand the pawn structure if White exchanges.
steps.position: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bc4 Bc5 d3 Nf6 O-O d6 c3 O-O

steps.title: White supports the center
steps.text: Re1 adds support to e4. White can also prepare b4 to gain queenside space, so improving your remaining bishop should take that expansion into account.

steps.title: Restrain before exchanging
steps.text: Use the a-pawn to add control of b4 before developing the c8-bishop.
steps.feedback: a5 controls b4 alongside your c5-bishop. White develops Nbd2. The extra pawn control makes a queenside expansion harder to support, leaving you better placed to challenge White's active bishop.

steps.title: Challenge White's active bishop
steps.text: Develop the c8-bishop to a square where it attacks White's bishop on c4. Be ready to recapture if White chooses the exchange.
steps.feedback: Be6 challenges the bishop on c4. White can keep the bishops on the board, but chooses Bxe6 in our study line. First restore material before planning anything else.
steps.hint: Develop the bishop from c8 to e6.

steps.title: Accept a structural tradeoff
steps.text: Recapture White's bishop with your f-pawn. Then compare what the pawn move gains and what it gives up.
steps.feedback: Material is equal again. You have doubled e-pawns, but the new e6-pawn supports d5 and f5. Your f-file is semi-open: White still has a pawn on f2. An open line is a future resource, not an immediate attack.

steps.title: Read the position after the exchange
steps.text: Your a5-pawn restrains b4; it does not make that advance impossible. Your doubled e-pawns cannot defend each other, although e6 supports useful central squares. The f6-knight blocks your rook's route along the f-file, so the rook does not attack f2 yet. White still has c3 ready to support d4. If White keeps the bishops instead of exchanging, or changes the center, reassess rather than replaying this sequence automatically.

steps.title: Connect the plan to the tradeoff
steps.text: Recall just the new decisions from the castled position.

steps.title: When White opens the center early
steps.text: c3 alone does not promise an immediate attack: White can still play d3 and reach a quiet setup. This chapter examines d4 before castling instead. Meet the pawn contact, save your attacked bishop with check and look for your own d5 break.

steps.title: Recognize c3
steps.text: Return to the bishop-first Italian. White prepares d4 with c3.
steps.show: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bc4 Bc5 c3

steps.title: Develop against the center
steps.text: Develop the kingside knight and attack e4.
steps.feedback: White plays d4, attacking your e5-pawn and c5-bishop. The center now needs a concrete response. If White plays d3 instead, play d6 and castle: that leads back to your quiet setup.

steps.title: Resolve the pawn contact
steps.text: Capture the pawn that has advanced to d4.
steps.feedback: exd4 removes the pawn that attacked your bishop and e5-pawn.
steps.hint: The e5-pawn can capture on d4.

steps.title: If White pushes e5
steps.text: White usually takes back with cxd4. A side trip shows e5 first, which attacks your knight. Explore e5, or continue to the main line.

steps.title: White pushes e5 instead
steps.text: Instead of taking back on d4, White pushes e5 and attacks your f6-knight.

steps.title: Counterattack the bishop
steps.text: Don't retreat the knight. Push your d-pawn two squares to attack the c4-bishop.
steps.feedback: d5 attacks the bishop, so if White takes your knight, you can take the bishop. White moves it to b5 instead, where it pins your c6-knight.

steps.title: Jump forward
steps.text: Your knight is still attacked. Move it forward to a central square your d5-pawn protects.
steps.feedback: On e4 the knight is safe and active. White takes back on d4, attacking your c5-bishop again.
steps.hint: Move the knight from f6 to e4.

steps.title: Keep the bishop
steps.text: Retreat the bishop one square along its diagonal, where it still eyes d4.
steps.feedback: Bb6 keeps the bishop safe and pressing on d4.
steps.hint: Move the bishop from c5 to b6.

steps.title: Active pieces
steps.text: Castle next. If White takes your c6-knight with check first, recapture with the b-pawn. Earlier, if White had taken your knight with exf6 or recaptured with cxd4, take the c4-bishop with dxc4; after exf6 dxc4, answer fxg7 with Rg8. If White had captured your d-pawn en passant with exd6, recapture with your queen. If the bishop had gone to b3 or e2 instead of b5, Ne4 was still the move.

steps.title: White takes back
steps.text: After cxd4, White has pawns on d4 and e4, and your bishop is attacked again by the new pawn on d4.

steps.title: Move the bishop with check
steps.text: Save the c5-bishop while making White answer a check.
steps.feedback: Bb4+ moves the bishop out of attack. White blocks the check with Bd2; we will exchange that bishop before breaking in the center. The next chapter covers blocking with Nc3 instead.

steps.title: Exchange the blocking bishop
steps.text: Capture the bishop on d2 with check. White can develop a knight while recapturing.
steps.feedback: Bxd2+ trades your bishop for White's and gives check.
steps.hint: Move the bishop from b4 to d2.

steps.title: If White recaptures with the queen
steps.text: The main line recaptures with the knight. Explore Qxd2, which leaves e4 without a defender, or continue to the main line.

steps.title: White recaptures with the queen
steps.text: Qxd2 takes back the bishop, but unlike Nbxd2 it leaves the e4-pawn without a defender.

steps.title: Take the loose pawn
steps.text: Capture the undefended e4-pawn with your knight.
steps.feedback: Nxe4 wins a pawn. White's Qe3 attacks the knight and pins it to your king on e8.
steps.hint: Capture on e4 with the knight from f6.

steps.title: Defend the pinned knight
steps.text: Your e4-knight cannot move while it shields your king. Support it with a pawn.
steps.feedback: d5 defends the knight and attacks the c4-bishop. You are a pawn ahead.

steps.title: A pawn ahead
steps.text: Castle next, which ends the pin. If White first pins your c6-knight with Bb5, break that pin with Bd7, then castle; if White's bishop takes on d5, recapture with the queen. Earlier, if White's queen had gone to f4 or e2 instead of e3, d5 was still the move.

steps.title: White recaptures with the knight
steps.text: After Nbxd2, each side has traded a bishop. Your d-pawn can now challenge White's center.

steps.title: Challenge both central targets
steps.text: Advance your d-pawn two squares, attacking e4 and the bishop on c4.
steps.feedback: d5 challenges White's center immediately. White captures; our next move restores the material balance.

steps.title: Recapture with a piece
steps.text: Restore the material balance with a knight and occupy the square in front of White's d-pawn.
steps.feedback: Nxd5 restores equal material and places a knight in the center.

steps.title: If White checks with the queen
steps.text: White's main line here is castling. Side trips show Qe2+ and Qb3 first. Explore Qe2+, or continue to the next reply.

steps.title: White checks on the e-file
steps.text: Qe2+ uses the open e-file to check your king.

steps.title: Block with the bishop
steps.text: Block the check with a piece that develops and also guards your d5-knight.
steps.feedback: Be6 blocks the check and defends d5. Avoid Qe7: your queen would stop guarding d5, and Bxd5 would win the knight. White castles.
steps.hint: Move the bishop from c8 to e6.

steps.title: Castle
steps.text: Your king is still on the e-file. Castle.
steps.feedback: Both kings are castled and material is level.

steps.title: The same plan
steps.text: White's d4-pawn is isolated, as in the main line: keep your knight on d5 and aim at d4. Earlier, if White had taken on d5 instead of castling, recapture with the queen, because your e6-bishop is pinned. If White had attacked that bishop with Ng5, take the knight with your queen: nothing defends it. If White had played Ne5, take the d4-pawn with your c6-knight, which also attacks the queen.

steps.title: If White plays Qb3
steps.text: Explore Qb3, which lines the queen up behind the bishop against d5, or continue to the main line.

steps.title: White doubles up on d5
steps.text: Qb3 lines up behind the c4-bishop against your d5-knight and also attacks b7.

steps.title: Add a defender
steps.text: Move your c6-knight to a square where it also defends d5.
steps.feedback: Nce7 defends d5 a second time, and your c8-bishop still guards b7. White castles.
steps.hint: Move the knight from c6 to e7.

steps.title: Castle
steps.text: d5 and b7 are covered. Castle.
steps.feedback: Both kings are castled and material is level.

steps.title: Hold d5
steps.text: Keep the knight on d5 and aim at White's isolated d4-pawn, as in the main line. Na5 was the other good answer to Qb3, attacking the queen and bishop: if White checks with Qa4+, Nc6 returns, and the same moves can repeat.

steps.title: White castles
steps.text: White castles. Now attend to your own king.

steps.title: Castle after the exchanges
steps.text: The kingside route is clear. Castle before deciding where your remaining bishop belongs.
steps.feedback: Both kings are castled and material is level. The exchanges have left a useful structural target to understand before you continue.

steps.title: Play against the isolated d-pawn
steps.text: White's d4-pawn has no friendly pawn on the c- or e-file to protect it. Your knight on d5 blocks its advance. Keep control of d5, finish developing and look for pressure on d4. Safe piece exchanges can reduce White's activity, but the pawn also gives White space and control of e5: it is a target, not a pawn you have already won.

steps.title: A different reply to the bishop check
steps.text: Steinitz–von Bardeleben, Hastings 1895. White blocks Bb4+ with Nc3 instead of Bd2, and Black answers d5. Stockfish prefers Nxe4 there, which the next chapter teaches. The later Black loss is not part of your taught line.

steps.title: Meet c3 and d4
steps.text: Play the studied response to the central advance.

steps.title: White blocks the check with a knight
steps.text: We return to the bishop check from the previous chapter. Instead of Bd2, White can block with Nc3 and offer the e4-pawn. Taking it is the only good answer, and it leads to sharp, well-known lines.
steps.position: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bc4 Bc5 c3 Nf6 d4 exd4 cxd4 Bb4+

steps.title: The knight blocks the check
steps.text: Nc3 blocks the check and develops, but your b4-bishop pins the knight to White's king.

steps.title: Take the e4-pawn
steps.text: The pinned c3-knight cannot recapture on e4. Take the pawn with your knight.
steps.feedback: Nxe4 wins a pawn and attacks the pinned c3-knight a second time. Castling or Bxc3+ instead gives White the better game.
steps.hint: Capture on e4 with the knight from f6.

steps.title: If White pins your knight with Qe2
steps.text: In this chapter's main line, White castles and gives up more material. A side trip shows Qe2 first. Explore Qe2, or continue to the main line.

steps.title: White pins your knight
steps.text: Qe2 attacks your e4-knight and pins it to your king.

steps.title: Support the knight
steps.text: Defend the e4-knight with a pawn that also attacks the c4-bishop.
steps.feedback: d5 defends the knight and attacks the bishop. White moves it to b5, where it pins your c6-knight too.

steps.title: Castle out of both pins
steps.text: Castle: your king leaves the e-file and the b5-bishop's diagonal.
steps.feedback: Neither of your knights is pinned any more, and you are a pawn ahead.

steps.title: White's king is still in the center
steps.text: Your king is safe, while White's c3-knight is still pinned and attacked twice. Earlier, if White had played Bb3 instead of Bb5, castle too, and if the bishop had taken on d5, recapture with your queen. If White had castled instead of moving the bishop, take the c3-knight with your bishop first.

steps.title: White castles and offers more
steps.text: White castles, so the c3-knight is no longer pinned. This is a gambit: White gives up material to open lines while your king is still in the center.

steps.title: Take the knight
steps.text: Capture the c3-knight with your bishop. Castling first would let it jump to d5 and attack your bishop.
steps.feedback: Bxc3 removes the knight before it can join the attack.
steps.hint: Capture on c3 with the bishop from b4.

steps.title: If White pushes d5
steps.text: The main line recaptures with bxc3. A side trip shows d5, the Møller Attack. Explore d5, or continue to the main line.

steps.title: The Møller Attack
steps.text: White leaves your bishop on c3 and pushes d5, attacking your c6-knight.

steps.title: Bring the bishop back
steps.text: White can still take your c3-bishop. Retreat it to f6, near your king.
steps.feedback: Bf6 saves the bishop. White takes your c6-knight with the pawn.
steps.hint: Move the bishop from c3 to f6.

steps.title: Take back
steps.text: Recapture the pawn on c6.
steps.feedback: bxc6 leaves you two pawns ahead.
steps.hint: Capture on c6 with the b7-pawn.

steps.title: Two pawns ahead
steps.text: White is ahead in development in return for the pawns, so castle soon. Earlier, if White had played Re1 instead of dxc6, move your c6-knight to e7; after Rxe4, castle.

steps.title: White recaptures
steps.text: White takes back with the b-pawn. Next White wants Re1, pinning your e4-knight to your king.

steps.title: Support the knight
steps.text: Push your d-pawn two squares: it defends the e4-knight and attacks the c4-bishop.
steps.feedback: d5 defends e4 and attacks the bishop. White moves it to b5, pinning your c6-knight.

steps.title: Castle
steps.text: Get your king out of the pin and off the e-file before White's rook arrives.
steps.feedback: Your king is safe and neither knight is pinned. You are a pawn ahead.

steps.title: A pawn ahead
steps.text: White has two bishops and open lines for the pawn, so keep your pieces active: develop the c8-bishop next. Against Bb3, Bd3 or Re1 instead of Bb5, castling is also good. Against Ba3, which stops you castling, take the c4-bishop with dxc4.

steps.title: Meet Nc3
steps.text: Play the line against Nc3 from the bishop check.

steps.title: You do not have to accept the gambit
steps.text: The Evans Gambit offers b4 to draw your bishop away and gain time for a central expansion. Here we decline with Bb6. White keeps extra queenside space, so the bishop still needs a safe retreat.

steps.title: White offers the b-pawn
steps.text: The pawn on b4 attacks your bishop on c5. We will move the bishop instead of capturing it.
steps.show: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bc4 Bc5 b4

steps.title: Decline without abandoning the diagonal
steps.text: Retreat the bishop one square along the a7–g1 diagonal.
steps.feedback: Bb6 preserves the bishop without taking a pawn. White's c3 prepares d4; declining has not stopped White from building a center.

steps.title: Support your center
steps.text: Support e5 with the d-pawn before White expands further.
steps.feedback: d6 supports e5. White advances a4 and can push a5 to attack your bishop.

steps.title: Make a retreat square
steps.text: White threatens to gain time with a5. Use your a-pawn to make a safe retreat square for the bishop.
steps.feedback: a6 vacates a7. White pushes a5 and attacks the bishop on b6.

steps.title: Use the space you prepared
steps.text: Retreat the attacked bishop to a7.
steps.feedback: The bishop is safe on a7. White has more queenside space; you can return to development as the next moves allow.

steps.title: White can keep pushing or develop
steps.text: The main line continues with d3 and castling. Explore White's b5 advance, which Pollock played against Lasker, or continue to the main line.

steps.title: White pushes the b-pawn again
steps.text: Pollock played b5 against Lasker. The pawn attacks your c6-knight, but your a6-pawn can take it.

steps.title: Take the pawn
steps.text: Capture the b5-pawn with your a-pawn.
steps.feedback: axb5 removes the attacker. White's bishop takes back on b5 and pins your c6-knight to your king.
steps.hint: Capture on b5 with the a6-pawn.

steps.title: Develop with an attack
steps.text: Develop your kingside knight, attacking e4.
steps.feedback: Nf6 develops and attacks e4. White pushes a6 instead of defending it.

steps.title: Take the loose pawn
steps.text: Nothing defends e4. Take it.
steps.feedback: Nxe4 wins a pawn. In Pollock–Lasker, Black castled here instead, which is also good.
steps.hint: Capture on e4 with the knight from f6.

steps.title: A pawn ahead
steps.text: Castle next, but if White's queen attacks your knight from e2, retreat it to f6 first. If White takes on b7 with the a-pawn, recapture with the c8-bishop. Return to the branch point to practice the quieter continuation.

steps.title: White returns to development
steps.text: White supports e4 with d3 instead of pushing another queenside pawn. Return to your own development now that the bishop is safe.

steps.title: Finish clearing the castling route
steps.text: Develop the remaining kingside knight toward the center. White's d3-pawn protects e4, so the attack on e4 is pressure rather than a free pawn.
steps.feedback: Nf6 clears g8. White castles; you have no piece left between your king and h8-rook either.
steps.hint: Develop the knight from g8 to f6.

steps.title: Secure the king before a central break
steps.text: Use the route you have prepared to bring your king to safety.
steps.feedback: Both kings are castled. White has queenside space, but you have finished kingside development without losing material. Look next for chances to challenge the center, as the historical example illustrates.
steps.hint: Castle kingside by moving e8 to g8.

steps.title: Answer flank space with central activity
steps.text: Pollock–Lasker, Hastings 1895. White pushes the queenside pawns. Black preserves the bishop, castles and develops; then d5 challenges e4 while White's king is still in the center. Watch how the prepared break gives Black active play instead of endlessly defending the queenside.

steps.title: Decline and finish developing
steps.text: Play the quieter continuation you studied.
